Overview of Resuscitation Framework
General CPR Master Overview
WHAT is Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR)?

Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR) is a universal emergency procedure designed to manually keep a person alive when their heart stops beating and their breathing ceases. The term itself explains exactly what it does: "Cardio" (heart), "Pulmonary" (lungs), and "Resuscitation" (reviving). By physically pushing down on a casualty's chest, you act as their mechanical heart pump to circulate blood; by blowing air into their mouth, you act as their mechanical lungs to supply oxygen.
WHY must you understand the General Procedure?

The Brain’s Countdown: The human brain cannot survive without oxygen. Within 4 to 6 minutes of a stopped heart, brain damage begins. By 10 minutes, the brain dies completely. CPR acts as a placeholder to delay this countdown.

Simplifying the Chaos: In a real emergency, panic sets in easily. Understanding this singular, overarching framework ensures that no matter what age the casualty is, your brain defaults to a clear, logical step-by-step checklist.
WHO does this general framework apply to?

This master framework applies to every human being who is found unconscious, unresponsive, and either not breathing or gasping abnormally. While the physical strength and hand placements shift depending on the casualty's size, the underlying diagnostic steps and safety rules remain identical across all age groups:
Adults: Ages 8 and above. Requires two hands and deep, powerful compressions.
Children: Ages 1 to puberty. Requires one or two hands with moderate depth adjustments.
Infants: Under 1 year old. Requires delicate 2-finger compressions and specialized breathing seals.
Neonates: Newborns under 28 days old. Focuses heavily on highly synchronized 3:1 ratio cycles.
WHEN should you act, adapt, or stop?
When to Act: The moment you determine a person does not respond to touch/sound AND their chest is not rising normally.
When to Adapt: You must instantly adapt your physical compression force based on who is in front of you (Adults: 5–6 cm; Children: 5 cm; Infants/Neonates: 3–4 cm).
WHEN to Stop: You only stop when professional medical aid takes over, an AED explicitly tells you to clear the body, the person revives, or you become completely physically exhausted.
WHERE is the ideal CPR environment?
Safety First: The immediate structural location must be entirely hazard-free. Never attempt CPR in the middle of a busy road, inside a burning room, or on an unstable unstable cliff edge.

The Hard Ground Rule: To make chest compressions work, the casualty’s back must be pressed against a rigid, unyielding surface. Performing CPR on soft mattresses or couches will fail because the springs will bounce and absorb your depth.

HOW to Navigate: Universal DRSABCD
Follow this uniform sequence to safely systematically manage any casualty.
Step 1: D – Danger

Before rushing in, check for physical hazards or personal threats (live wires, fires, unstable glass). If the environment is safe, move trivial obstacles like chairs or bags completely away from the body to establish a clean, open 360-degree workspace.
Step 2: R – Response

Determine consciousness by shouting loudly into both ears and firmly tapping their shoulders (or flicking foot soles for infants). Shout: "Hello! Can you hear me?!" If there is zero response, eye flickers, or body shifts, proceed immediately.
Step 3: S – Send for Help

Call your local emergency number. If alone, immediately switch your phone onto loudspeaker and place it right beside the casualty's head. Talk to the dispatcher hands-free while your arms remain clear to perform lifesaving actions.
Step 4: A – Airway
The Check: Inspect the inner mouth. If any fluid, blood, or food is visible, tilt their head to the side and clear it with a careful finger sweep.

The Tilt: Perform the Head-Tilt, Chin-Lift maneuver by placing one hand flat on the forehead and two fingers under the chin bone, gently lifting to pull the tongue away from the windpipe throat. (Keep neutral for newborns/infants).
Step 5: B – Check for Breathing
Put your ear close to their mouth and nose while watching the chest area. Evaluate for no more than 10 seconds checking for three actions simultaneously:
Look: Check if the chest rises up and falls back down smoothly.
Listen: Listen directly for normal, steady breathing sounds.
Feel: Feel for air streams against your cheek.
Critical Note: Infrequent, irregular snoring gasps are NOT normal breathing signs. Treat it as cardiac arrest and start compressions immediately.
Step 6: C – Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation
Position your shoulders directly above your hands, lock your elbows completely straight, and push straight down using your body mass at a uniform speed of 100 to 120 actions per minute.
Ratios: Adults, children, and infants receive a loop of 30 compressions and 2 breaths. Neonates shift to a tight 3:1 ratio configuration.
Hands-Only Modification: If you are uncomfortable or lack a rescue barrier mask, skip breaths completely and deliver continuous chest compressions.
Step 7: D – Defibrillation

Turn on an Automated External Defibrillator (AED) as soon as it arrives. The machine handles the processing steps automatically and speaks directions aloud. Follow the pads visual diagram or spoken audio guides flawlessly. Do not look for an AED if resuscitating a newborn under 28 days old.
